In the Node.js server process, `src/instrumentation.ts` runs `register()`. It imports `registerEventHandlers()` from `src/server/services/event-registry.ts`, then starts the scheduler with `startScheduler()` from `src/server/jobs/scheduler.ts`. The registry imports `notification-service.ts`, which registers the `issue.overdue` subscriber when the module loads.

`startScheduler()` sets an interval that calls `tick(new Date())` once a minute. In `tick()`, the `overdue-issues` job is due immediately on its first pass and then once per hour, according to `CADENCE_MINUTES`. The scheduler enqueues it and `drain()` dispatches it through `runHandler()` in `src/server/jobs/queue.ts`, which calls `runOverdueIssueJob()` in `src/server/jobs/overdue-issue-job.ts`. There is also a separate cron route, `POST` in `src/app/api/cron/overdue/route.ts`, which checks the cron secret and calls the same runner.

The runner checks `shouldFilterArchived(LIVE_ONLY)` before scanning. It gets up to 50 organization IDs from `usageRepo.listOrgIdsForRollup()`, then calls `issueRepo.listOverdueIssues(orgId, stamp)` for each. That repository query narrows the set to live issues in the organization with a non-null due date earlier than the current timestamp and a status of `backlog`, `todo`, `in_progress`, or `in_review`. Completed and canceled issues do not qualify. The runner also skips any returned issue whose `dueAt` is null.

The job’s responsibility is to announce that an issue is overdue, not to create or deliver notifications. For each qualifying issue it hasn’t announced before, it emits `issue.overdue` with the organization, issue, project, due date, and assignee IDs. After `emit()` succeeds, the runner adds the issue ID to the module-level `reported` set. That set suppresses repeat announcements on later passes during the same process lifetime; it is in-memory, so a process restart clears it. `resetOverdueTracking()` exists for tests.

The notification subscriber in `src/server/services/notification-service.ts` ignores events without an assignee. Otherwise it calls `notify()` with that one assignee as the recipient and kind `issue_overdue`. `notify()` deduplicates recipient IDs, skips the actor if applicable, looks up that person’s preference for this notification kind, and resolves their channels with `resolveChannels()`. If they have no explicit preference, the default is in-app and email. An explicit preference can turn either channel off; `digestOnly` suppresses immediate email when the `digest_email` feature is enabled. If all channels are off, no row is created. Otherwise `notify()` inserts a notification row for that recipient through `notificationRepo.insertNotifications()`.

The row is what delivers the in-app alert to that person’s notification list and bell. Email is preference-controlled through the row’s channel selection: for digest-only preferences, `runDigestEmailJob()` gathers that recipient’s unread notifications and, when the organization’s digest hour and plan flag allow it, sends a digest through `sendEmail()` in `src/server/services/email-service.ts`. This project’s `sendEmail()` writes the email draft to the structured log rather than using an outbound mail transport.
